intro: Pange lingua gloriosi corporis mysterium is a traditional plainchant hymn in six Latin stanzas on the bread and wine of the Eucharist. It is monophonic, a single melody with no separate accompaniment, and is sung here by Gareth Hughes.

sections.label: A′ · More verses of the same tune
sections.mNote: New Latin words fill the familiar phrases.

sections.label: A″ · Closing stanzas, same melody
sections.mNote: The same voice sings the final stanzas to the same melody.

cues.title: Gareth Hughes, solo voice
cues.text: Gareth Hughes sings the traditional Roman melody in Mode III, also called Phrygian. He sings unaccompanied.
cues.evidence: The recording description identifies Gareth Hughes and Mode III. The hymn’s music history identifies this as the Roman Phrygian tune. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pange_Lingua_Latin_in_Latin.ogg ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pange_lingua_gloriosi_corporis_mysterium

cues.title: Aquinas’s text, stanzas three and four
cues.text: Thomas Aquinas’s thirteenth-century hymn describes Christ at table with the twelve apostles, giving himself to them as food with his own hands. The Latin text centres on bread, flesh, wine and blood.
cues.evidence: Aquinas’s text, especially stanzas three and four; Hugh Henry, “Pange Lingua Gloriosi”, The Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), section on the hymn of Aquinas. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11441c.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pange_lingua_gloriosi_corporis_mysterium

cues.title: Strophic form, six stanzas
cues.text: Each of the six stanzas has six lines and is sung to the same tune. The Latin text turns first to the body and blood, then to Christ’s birth, the Last Supper and the act of worship.
cues.evidence: The complete six-stanza Latin text and traditional chant setting are reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pange_lingua_gloriosi_corporis_mysterium ; Hughes’s recording uses the traditional Latin text.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Text of the Tantum ergo
cues.text: The final two stanzas are also sung on their own as Tantum ergo at Benediction. In them Aquinas calls on the worshippers to kneel, and he ends with praise of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
cues.evidence: Hugh Henry, “Pange Lingua Gloriosi”, The Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), on the separate use of the last two stanzas; the Latin text supplies their subjects. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11441c.htm
